title: Passwords: stop remembering them
subtitle: Four rules, and five accounts to put them to the test

cards.title: Only length slows the attacker down
cards.say: People hand me punctuation as if it were armour. The machine that guesses passwords doesn't care about your exclamation mark. What slows it down is the number of combinations it has to try.

rules.headline: Long beats clever.
rules.body: Four or five unrelated words. A short password stays short, however many symbols you stuff into it.

rules.headline: Never the same one twice.
rules.body: A leak on one site turns into five on its own: attackers try the username-and-password pairs they already have everywhere else.

cards.sign_off: Four unrelated words beat P@ssw0rd! by a margin no punctuation can make up.

cards.title: The part nobody wants to hear
cards.say: Nobody's asking you to remember them, and the arithmetic is on your side: no one keeps forty different passwords in their head. So people reuse one, and that's the whole problem right there.

rules.headline: Leave yourself out of it.
rules.body: Your first name, your year of birth, your cat's name, your favourite team. All of it is already lying around online, and it's the first thing anyone tries.

rules.headline: Remembering is the manager's job.
rules.body: You remember one strong passphrase, and it keeps all the rest.

cards.sign_off: One strong passphrase, a manager for the rest, and multi-factor authentication wherever it's offered.

sections.intro: Now for the part that actually fixes it. Pick one now, while you're here: any of them beats your memory, and four of the five are free.

tools.name: Bitwarden
tools.what: Free, open source, audited, syncs across all your devices.
tools.dog_says: My oldest companion. He remembers everything for you and only offers your login on the real site. If he offers nothing, take a closer look at the address.

tools.name: Proton Pass
tools.what: Swiss, free plan, same account as Proton Mail.
tools.dog_says: Newer than the others, and based here in Switzerland. A good pick if you already use their mail.

tools.name: KeePassXC
tools.what: Everything stays in a file on your own device. No company between you and your passwords.
tools.dog_says: For people who trust nobody. Fair enough. But the backups are your job too.

tools.name: 1Password
tools.what: Paid, and the easiest to set up for a whole family.
tools.dog_says: It costs money, I won't hide that. Worth it if you're setting up your parents too.

tools.name: The one already on your phone
tools.what: Apple Passwords, Google Password Manager or Firefox.
tools.dog_says: Already there, already backed up, nothing to install. The catch: it ties you to one ecosystem, which makes things awkward if you switch phones. Still far better than reusing a password.

sections.question: How are you feeling about all this?

levels.label: Still unsure
levels.reply: That's perfectly fine. Just one thing today: install one of the managers Dog showed you. The rest will follow, and we'll take it slowly.

levels.label: Getting there
levels.reply: Good. Prove it on five accounts in a row: that's where memory gives out.

levels.label: Confident
levels.reply: Ah, confidence. Then five accounts won't give you any trouble. I'll be waiting at the end to show you which one I'd have cracked first.

cards.title: Now, the proof
cards.say: Knowing the rules costs nothing. Five accounts in a row is another matter: around the third, your memory gives up and only the manager is left. You can't learn this one by reading. You have to feel it happen.

rules.headline: Five sites, five new passwords.
rules.body: All made up, all ours, and they unlock nothing. Don't use any of your real passwords, not even once.

rules.headline: Save them as you go.
rules.body: In the manager you've just installed. Not in a note, not in your head.

rules.headline: We'll ask for one of them back.
rules.body: In a later session, one of the five, picked at random. We won't say which, so you'll need to have saved them all. And we can't remind you, because we never kept them.

cards.sign_off: Five accounts. Then we'll know whether the habit is real.
